title: Palestinian-Style Musakhan with Sumac Chicken & Onion Flatbread
dek: Roasted chicken quarters rest on olive-oil-soaked flatbreads under a generous layer of jammy sumac onions, toasted pine nuts and parsley.
image_alt: Roasted sumac chicken quarters on round flatbreads covered with purple-red onions, toasted pine nuts and chopped parsley
ingredients: 3 whole chicken leg quarters, about 3 1/2 lb total, separated into thighs and drumsticks
2 tbsp ground sumac, divided, plus more for serving
4 large red onions, halved and thinly sliced, about 2 lb
1/2 cup low-sodium chicken stock or water
6 round pocketless flatbreads, such as taboon, naan or thick pita, 7 to 8 inches each

instructions.name: Season the chicken
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 425°F with a rack in the upper third. Pat the chicken dry. Mix 1 1/2 teaspoons salt, pepper, 1 tablespoon sumac, allspice and cinnamon, then rub the mixture and 1 tablespoon olive oil over every piece. Arrange skin-side up on a rimmed sheet pan.

instructions.name: Roast to a safe temperature
instructions.text: Roast the chicken for 35 to 45 minutes, rotating the pan once, until deeply browned and the thickest part of every thigh and drumstick reaches at least 165°F without the thermometer touching bone. For the most tender dark meat, 175 to 185°F is ideal. Transfer the chicken to a clean plate and reserve the pan juices.

instructions.name: Cook the sumac onions
instructions.text: While the chicken roasts, warm 4 tablespoons olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-low heat. Add the onions and remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt. Cook for 25 to 30 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until collapsed and jammy but not crisp. Stir in the remaining 1 tablespoon sumac and the stock; simmer for 3 minutes, until glossy.

instructions.name: Toast the pine nuts
instructions.text: Set a small dry skillet over medium-low heat. Toast the pine nuts for 3 to 5 minutes, stirring constantly once they begin to color, until evenly golden. Immediately tip them onto a plate so the residual heat does not burn them.

instructions.name: Build the flatbreads
instructions.text: Lower the oven to 375°F. Brush the flatbreads with the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil and arrange them, slightly overlapping if needed, on a clean sheet pan. Spoon the onions and their oil evenly over the breads, leaving a narrow rim. Bake for 7 to 9 minutes, until the bottoms are warm and lightly crisp while the centers remain pliable.

instructions.name: Finish like the photographed platter
instructions.text: Move the onion-covered flatbreads to a large platter and set one chicken piece on each. Spoon over the reserved roasting juices, then scatter with pine nuts, parsley and an extra pinch of sumac. Serve immediately with lemon wedges, tearing the flatbread into portions at the table.

why_it_works: Drying and roasting the chicken separately preserves crisp skin while the bone-in pieces stay juicy enough to season the bread with their drippings.
Slow-cooked onions absorb sumac and olive oil, creating the tangy, savory layer that defines the dish without turning the flatbread soggy.
A short final bake warms and lightly crisps the bread before it receives the chicken, pine nuts and fresh parsley shown in the licensed photograph.
swaps: Use six bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs of similar size; begin checking at 30 minutes and cook every piece to at least 165°F.
If pine nuts are unavailable, use toasted slivered almonds. For a nut-free meal, substitute toasted pumpkin seeds and disclose the change to diners.
Taboon is traditional, but sturdy pocketless pita or naan works well. Avoid very thin lavash, which softens too quickly under the onions and juices.
storage: Remove chicken from the bread before storing. Cool everything within 2 hours and refrigerate chicken and onions together in a shallow airtight container for up to 4 days; wrap the flatbreads separately for up to 2 days. Reheat chicken and onions covered at 350°F until the chicken reaches 165°F, about 12 to 15 minutes. Warm the bread uncovered for the last 4 minutes. Freeze the chicken and onions, but not the assembled bread, for up to 2 months.
notes: Sumac should taste bright and tart, not dusty or bitter. Store it airtight away from heat and replace it when its color and aroma fade.
The onions need patient medium-low heat: browning them hard makes the topping sweet and crisp instead of soft, tangy and oil-rich.
The calorie and cost estimates include one chicken piece, one flatbread, onion topping and pine nuts per serving.

faqs.q: Can I assemble musakhan ahead of time?
faqs.a: Cook the chicken and onions up to one day ahead, but keep them separate from the bread. Reheat both to 165°F, warm the flatbreads, then assemble just before serving so the bread stays pliable at the center and lightly crisp at the edges.

faqs.q: Why are my onions dry instead of jammy?
faqs.a: The heat was likely too high or the pan too narrow. Lower the heat, add 2 tablespoons water and continue stirring until the onions collapse. Their texture should be soft and glossy before the sumac and stock go in.

faqs.q: Does the chicken have to reach 185°F?
faqs.a: No. Poultry is safe at 165°F, measured away from the bone. Dark meat becomes more tender as connective tissue softens around 175 to 185°F, so that higher range is a texture target rather than the minimum safety temperature.

title: Flaky Chinese Scallion Pancakes with Crisp Golden Layers
dek: Hot-water dough, toasted sesame oil and abundant scallions roll into savory spirals that pan-fry crisp outside and chewy within.
image_alt: Four rustic round scallion pancakes with browned blistered surfaces and visible green onion pieces on a white plate
image_credit: Infrogmation of New Orleans / Wikimedia Commons
ingredients: 3 1/3 cups all-purpose flour, 400 g, plus more for dusting
1/4 cup room-temperature water, 60 g, plus 1 tbsp if needed
1/3 cup all-purpose flour, 40 g, for the oil paste
8 scallions, green and pale parts very thinly sliced, about 1 1/2 cups
1/3 cup neutral oil, such as canola, for pan-frying
2 tbsp low-sodium soy sauce, optional for serving
1 tbsp rice vinegar, optional for serving

instructions.name: Make the hot-water dough
instructions.text: Place 400 grams flour and 1/2 teaspoon salt in a heat-safe bowl. Pour in the boiling water while stirring with chopsticks or a fork until shaggy. Add the room-temperature water and knead in the bowl for 3 minutes, until no dry flour remains. Add the final tablespoon water only if the dough will not come together.

instructions.name: Rest until extensible
instructions.text: Cover the dough and rest for 30 minutes. Knead on a lightly floured surface for 2 to 3 minutes, until smooth, then cover and rest 15 minutes more. This two-stage rest lets the hot-water dough roll thin without springing back.

instructions.name: Mix the oil paste
instructions.text: Stir the 40 grams flour, sesame oil and remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt into a smooth, pourable paste. Divide the dough into four equal pieces, about 175 grams each, and keep three covered while working with one.

instructions.name: Laminate with scallions
instructions.text: Roll one piece into a very thin 9-by-14-inch rectangle. Spread with one quarter of the sesame paste and scatter with one quarter of the scallions, leaving a 1-inch border along one long edge. Roll tightly from the opposite long edge into a rope, pinch the seam, then coil the rope into a snail. Tuck the end underneath. Repeat with the remaining dough and rest the four covered coils for 15 minutes.

instructions.name: Roll and pan-fry
instructions.text: Gently roll each coil into an 8-inch round about 1/4 inch thick. Heat 1 tablespoon neutral oil in a 10- or 12-inch skillet over medium. Fry one pancake for 3 to 4 minutes per side, adjusting the heat so it becomes golden and crisp without scorching. Add a little fresh oil for each pancake.

instructions.name: Vent, tear and serve
instructions.text: Transfer each pancake to a rack for 2 minutes so steam does not soften the underside. Clap it gently between clean hands or squeeze the edges inward with tongs to loosen the layers, then tear or cut into rustic pieces like the photographed plate. If desired, mix the soy sauce and vinegar and serve it in a separate small bowl.

why_it_works: Boiling water partially gelatinizes the flour, limiting gluten strength so the dough stays tender even after repeated rolling.
Flour thickens the sesame oil into a paste that remains in distinct sheets instead of squeezing out as the dough is coiled.
Rolling, coiling and rerolling creates many scallion-studded layers; resting between stages prevents shrinkage and torn surfaces.
swaps: Use half all-purpose and half bread flour for a chewier pancake, but expect the dough to need the full extra tablespoon of water and a longer rest.
Replace toasted sesame oil with neutral oil for a milder flavor; do not use butter because its water content can make the layers gummy.
For a gentler onion flavor, use mostly scallion greens. Chives can replace up to half the scallions but should not be the only allium.
storage: Cool cooked pancakes completely and refrigerate between parchment in an airtight container for up to 4 days. Reheat in a dry skillet over medium for 2 to 3 minutes per side or in a 375°F oven for 6 to 8 minutes; avoid the microwave, which makes the layers leathery. Freeze uncooked rolled rounds between parchment for up to 2 months and cook from frozen over medium-low, adding 2 to 3 minutes per side.
notes: Weighing the flour and water is especially helpful here because a stiff dough resists thin rolling while a wet dough leaks the sesame paste.
Use medium heat and let each side brown gradually; very high heat scorches the outside before the layered center cooks through.
The licensed photograph shows rustic whole pancakes with irregular, deeply browned patches and visible scallions; this recipe preserves that home-style presentation.

faqs.q: Why did my scallion pancakes lose their layers?
faqs.a: The sesame paste may have been too thin, the dough may not have rested, or the coil was rolled with excessive pressure. Use the flour-thickened paste, complete both rests and roll the final coil from the center outward with gentle, even strokes.

faqs.q: Can I prepare the dough the night before?
faqs.a: Yes. After the first 30-minute rest, coat the dough lightly with oil, cover airtight and refrigerate overnight. Let it stand at room temperature for 30 minutes before kneading briefly, dividing and laminating.

faqs.q: How do I keep multiple pancakes crisp for serving?
faqs.a: Hold them on a wire rack in a 250°F oven for up to 25 minutes. Do not stack or cover them, because trapped steam softens the browned surfaces.

title: Classic Canadian Butter Tarts with Raisins
dek: Flaky hand-cut pastry cups hold a glossy brown-sugar filling that bakes with caramelized tops, soft centers and plump raisins.
image_alt: Nine rustic Canadian butter tarts with flaky golden pastry, glossy brown-sugar filling and visible raisins on a wooden board
ingredients: 3/4 cup cold unsalted butter, 170 g, cut into 1/2-inch cubes
1/2 cup unsalted butter, 113 g, melted and cooled slightly
1 cup packed dark brown sugar, 210 g

instructions.name: Cut the pastry
instructions.text: Whisk the flour, granulated sugar and 1/2 teaspoon salt in a bowl. Cut in the cold butter with a pastry blender until pea-size pieces remain. Drizzle in 5 tablespoons ice water and toss; add more water 1 tablespoon at a time just until the dough holds when squeezed. Press into a disk, wrap and refrigerate for 45 minutes.

instructions.name: Plump the raisins
instructions.text: Cover the raisins with the boiling water and let them stand for 10 minutes. Drain thoroughly, spread on a clean towel and blot dry. Excess water can thin the filling and make the pastry bottoms soggy.

instructions.name: Line the muffin pan
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 400°F with a rack in the lower third. Roll the dough on a lightly floured surface to 1/8 inch thick. Cut twelve 4-inch rounds, rerolling scraps once. Ease each round into an ungreased standard metal muffin cup without stretching it. Chill the lined pan for 15 minutes.

instructions.name: Mix the filling gently
instructions.text: Whisk melted butter, brown sugar, maple syrup, eggs, vanilla, vinegar and remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt only until smooth; avoid beating in excess air. Divide the dry raisins among the shells, then add about 3 tablespoons filling to each, stopping 1/4 inch below the pastry rim.

instructions.name: Bake until deeply set at the edge
instructions.text: Set the muffin pan on a rimmed sheet pan and bake for 18 to 24 minutes, rotating once, until the pastry is golden, the filling is puffed at the edges and the centers still wobble slightly. An instant-read thermometer in a center should register at least 175°F; the filling will continue setting as it cools.

instructions.name: Cool before unmolding
instructions.text: Cool in the pan for 10 minutes. Run a thin offset spatula around any caramelized edges and lift the tarts to a rack before the sugar hardens against the pan. Cool at least 45 minutes for soft but sliceable centers like the photographed tarts.

why_it_works: Visible cold-butter pieces steam in the oven, creating a flaky shell sturdy enough to hold the fluid brown-sugar filling.
Maple syrup prevents graininess and adds flavor while a small amount of vinegar balances sweetness without making the filling sour.
Soaked, thoroughly dried raisins stay plump without releasing enough water to dilute the custard or soften the pastry.
swaps: Replace the raisins with 3/4 cup toasted chopped walnuts or pecans for a nut version; do not combine the full amounts or the cups can overflow.
Light brown sugar can replace dark brown sugar, producing a milder caramel flavor and slightly lighter filling.
For alcohol-free flavor variation, add 1/2 teaspoon maple extract. Do not replace maple syrup with straight granulated sugar, which changes both moisture and texture.
storage: Cool completely, then keep the tarts airtight at room temperature for 1 day or refrigerate for up to 5 days. Bring to room temperature or warm on a sheet pan at 300°F for 6 to 8 minutes; microwaving can make the pastry soft. Freeze in a single layer, then bag, for up to 2 months and thaw uncovered at room temperature.
notes: Place the muffin pan on a sheet pan before baking because a small amount of bubbling filling can caramelize over the edge.
Removing the tarts after 10 minutes is important: sooner can tear the hot pastry, while fully cooled sugar may glue the shells to the pan.
The licensed photograph shows rustic, hand-formed shells with glossy soft-set filling and visible raisins; perfectly smooth commercial tart shells are not the target.

faqs.q: Should butter tart filling be runny or firm?
faqs.a: This version is soft and gooey when fully cooled but should not pour out. For a firmer set, bake 2 to 3 minutes longer, until the center barely moves; for a softer set, remove the pan when the center still has a distinct wobble but is at least 175°F.

faqs.q: Why did my butter tarts overflow?
faqs.a: The shells were probably overfilled or the filling was whisked until foamy. Stop 1/4 inch below the rim, divide the mixture evenly and stir only until smooth. A metal muffin pan also transfers heat faster and controls the rise better than silicone.
Yes. Use enough refrigerated pie dough for two 9-inch crusts, roll it to about 1/8 inch and cut twelve 4-inch rounds. Keep the lined pan cold before filling and follow the same baking cues.
